title: New Coke
hook: It won the taste tests and lost the argument.
before: Pepsi had spent a decade running blind taste tests and gaining ground. Coca-Cola’s own research said a sweeter formula would beat both.
idea: On 23 April 1985 Coca-Cola replaced its formula with a new one, launched simply as the new Coke.
shift: People didn’t want a better taste. They wanted their Coke back. By June the consumer hotline was taking about 1,500 calls a day, and in July the company brought back the original as Coca-Cola Classic.
measure: The time from launch to the return of the original formula. A fact, not a result
evidence: Coca-Cola’s own history records the calls and the reversal. The company’s figures are self-reported, and no public source isolates the commercial cost.
lesson: Research can tell you what people prefer in a sip. It can’t tell you what they feel they own.
test: There is no effectiveness record. The evidence is the company’s account of calls, letters and the reversal.
links: See Coca-Cola’s 1985 launch advertisement · The Henry Ford
memorable: It is the rare failure that became a love letter. The anger proved how much the old brand meant.

creative.label: Watch CBS Evening News report drinkers’ reactions in 1985
creative.heading: Archive film

take: Read this next to the Pepsi Challenge in Edition 03. One sip of data pushed the biggest brand in the world into its biggest mistake.

image.alt: A red 1985 Coke can marked NEW
image.credit: New Coke can (1985) · CBS News archive feature

title: The Speech
hook: The boss called his own product crap, in public.
before: Gerald Ratner ran Britain’s biggest jewellery chain, built on cheap prices and a lot of shops.
idea: At the Institute of Directors in April 1991, he joked that one product was ‘total crap’ and that a prawn sandwich would outlast some of his earrings.
shift: Customers heard what he thought of them. The group’s value fell by around £500m, Ratner left, and the business was later renamed Signet.
measure: The approximate fall in the Ratner Group’s value, as widely reported
evidence: The fall in value is well documented, but the figure is approximate and the recession was hurting retailers at the same time.
lesson: People don’t only buy the product. They buy what it says about them.
test: The record is the company’s market value and what happened to the business afterwards.
memorable: It gave the language a phrase. ‘Doing a Ratner’ still means talking down your own business.

creative.label: Watch Gerald Ratner’s 1991 speech in the Institute of Directors archive
creative.heading: Campaign media

metric_label: Approximate fall in the group’s value
take: Ten seconds of honesty in the wrong room. It’s the clearest proof I know that a brand lives in the customer’s head, not the boardroom.

image.alt: Gerald Ratner speaking at the Institute of Directors’ 1991 convention
image.credit: Gerald Ratner at the 1991 Annual Convention · Institute of Directors archive

title: Free Flights
hook: Buy a vacuum cleaner, fly to America.
before: Hoover’s UK business had warehouses of stock to clear.
idea: In 1992 it offered two free return flights with any purchase over £100. Later that year the offer was extended to flights to the United States, worth far more than the machines.
shift: Far more people applied than Hoover had planned for. The flights cost far more than the sales earned, the complaints went on for years, and Hoover’s European business was later sold.
measure: One widely cited estimate of the cost. Sources put it at around £50m
evidence: The cost figures vary between sources, but all agree the promotion lost Hoover tens of millions of pounds and led to years of complaints.
lesson: An offer can’t be worth more than the thing it sells.
test: The record is the reported cost, the complaints and what happened to the business.
memorable: People bought vacuum cleaners they didn’t want to get a holiday they did.

creative.label: Watch Hoover’s 1992 Two Return Flights advert on The Laundry Lab
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: The most British failure in the edition. Everyone involved could do the sums, and nobody did.
data_source: The promotion ran away with the brand

title: Number Fever
hook: One number, printed on far too many caps.
before: Pepsi was well behind Coca-Cola in the Philippines and ran a bottle-cap contest to catch up.
idea: Number Fever promised cash prizes for caps printed with the winning number. When 349 was announced, huge numbers of people held a cap that seemed to win.
shift: Pepsi said most of those caps weren’t valid. Protests followed, some violent, and at least five people died. The lawsuits ran for years.
measure: Goodwill payments reported on Wikipedia. Other sources give different figures
evidence: The promotion is well recorded, but the figures for claims, payments and lawsuits vary between sources.
lesson: When a promise goes wrong at scale, the cost isn’t only money.
test: The record is the reported payments, lawsuits and the events that followed.
links: Licence for the 349 cap photograph · CC BY-SA 4.0
memorable: A three-digit number became shorthand for a corporate disaster.

creative.label: Watch Bloomberg Originals’ account of Number Fever and the 349 caps
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: The hardest case to include, and I nearly left it out. Marketing failures are usually embarrassing. This one cost lives.

image.alt: Inside of a Pepsi crown cap stamped 349 and Plays for 1 Million
image.credit: Geric Cruz, Pepsi Number Fever 349 cap · Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 · resized to WebP

title: Consignia
hook: The Post Office Group gave itself a new name. Nobody used it.
before: The Post Office Group was becoming a public limited company and wanted a name that sounded modern and international.
idea: In 2001 it renamed the group Consignia, keeping Royal Mail and Post Office as the brands people saw.
shift: The name was widely mocked and never caught on. In 2002, with the business losing money, the company announced it would become Royal Mail again.
measure: Roughly the time between the name’s introduction in January 2001 and the announcement in May 2002. A fact, not a result
evidence: Trade press records the name, the losses and the reversal. Reports put the cost of changing back at about £1m.
lesson: A name people already trust is an asset. Don’t trade it for one they have to learn.
test: The record is press coverage of the change and its reversal.
memorable: It is a word that sounds like a brand and means almost nothing.

creative.label: Watch ITN’s 2002 interview with Consignia chief executive John Roberts
creative.heading: Campaign media

metric_label: From launch to the reversal announcement
take: Every agency has a Consignia story. This is the one we all learned from.

title: The UK Launch
hook: Bottled tap water, then a recall.
before: Coca-Cola had built Dasani into a major bottled water brand in the United States and brought it to Britain in 2004.
idea: The launch called Dasani pure. The press soon reported that it was treated mains water from Sidcup, and British viewers remembered a sitcom joke about bottled tap water.
shift: Weeks later, tests found bromate above the legal limit in a batch. Coca-Cola recalled about 500,000 bottles and withdrew the brand from Britain.
measure: The number of bottles recalled in March 2004
evidence: The recall and withdrawal are well recorded. The launch failure combined a credibility problem with a quality one, and the record doesn’t separate the two.
lesson: If the story depends on purity, the product has to be beyond question.
test: The record is the recall, the withdrawal and press coverage.
memorable: It became the punchline the sitcom had already written.

creative.label: Watch Tom Scott revisit why the UK launch failed
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: Two problems at once. People might have forgiven the tap water, or the recall. Not both in five weeks.
data_source: Recalled and pulled from the UK

image.alt: Close-up of a blue Dasani label reading Pure, Still Water
image.credit: Dasani’s UK launch packaging (2004) · BBC News

title: The New Carton
hook: The orange with a straw disappeared, and so did the sales.
before: Tropicana Pure Premium was a market leader, recognised on the shelf by an orange with a straw in it.
idea: In January 2009 Arnell redesigned the carton with a glass of juice and a cleaner look, as part of a wider campaign.
shift: Shoppers couldn’t find their juice or thought it looked like an own label. Within two months PepsiCo announced the old carton would return.
measure: The fall in unit sales between 1 January and 22 February 2009, as reported from retail data
evidence: The sales fall is widely reported from retail data. It covers only seven weeks, and other factors weren’t separated out, so it is a trend rather than a modelled effect.
lesson: On a shelf, recognition is the product. Change the cues and you change what people think they’re buying.
test: Retail sales data tracked units before and after the change.
memorable: Everyone remembers the orange with the straw, which is exactly the point.

creative.label: Watch designer Peter Arnell explain the new carton to Ad Age in 2009
creative.heading: Campaign media

impact_source: Read the case · The Branding Journal
metric_label: Unit sales, in about seven weeks
take: The failure I quote most in meetings, because it has a number. A carton is a signpost before it is a design.

image.alt: Original orange-and-straw Tropicana carton beside the 2009 glass-of-juice redesign
image.credit: Tropicana, original and redesigned cartons (2009) · Brand New / UnderConsideration

title: Pizza Turnaround
hook: A pizza chain that told everyone its pizza was bad.
before: Domino’s had flat sales and a reputation for pizza that tasted like cardboard. It closed more than 100 US stores in 2009.
idea: Crispin Porter + Bogusky made a campaign that showed real focus groups criticising the pizza, then showed the company rebuilding the recipe.
shift: Admitting the problem made the new pizza believable.
measure: Domestic same-store sales growth reported in Domino’s first quarter 2010 earnings
evidence: Domino’s reported 14.3% same-store sales growth and credited the new pizza. That is a business trend. The recipe, the campaign and the price offers all changed together.
lesson: The fastest way back is to say what went wrong and show you fixed it.
test: The company’s quarterly earnings reported sales after the relaunch.
memorable: Seeing a chief executive watch customers call his pizza cardboard is still uncomfortable, and that’s why it works.

creative.label: Watch ‘Domino’s Pizza Turnaround’ on Domino’s channel

metric_label: US same-store sales, first quarter of 2010
take: The bravest brief in the edition. The failure was the pizza, and the brand fixed that before it made the ad.
data_source: Admitted it and fixed the pizza

image.alt: Two customers speaking in a Domino’s pizza focus group
image.credit: Domino’s and Crispin Porter + Bogusky, Pizza Turnaround · case-film still from D&AD

title: The New Logo
hook: A logo that lasted less than a week.
before: Gap’s blue box logo had been part of the brand for decades.
idea: In October 2010 Gap introduced a new logo, Helvetica with a small blue square, then invited the public to suggest alternatives.
shift: The response online was fierce and fast. Six days later Gap said it would return to the blue box.
measure: The time from the new logo’s launch to Gap’s reversal. A fact, not a result
evidence: The reversal is well recorded. No public source shows an effect on sales.
lesson: Social media gives people a vote, whether or not you asked for one.
test: The record is press coverage of the launch and the reversal.
links: Read Gap’s decision to restore the blue box
memorable: A parody account for the new logo became more famous than the logo.

creative.label: Watch branding practitioners discuss the Gap logo reversal
creative.heading: Campaign media

impact_source: Read the reversal report · CNN Money
metric_label: Before Gap brought back the old logo
take: The first rebrand to be marked live on social media. Asking for ideas after the backlash made it look worse.

image.alt: Gap’s 2010 Helvetica wordmark next to the classic blue square
image.credit: Gap’s 2010 and classic logos compared · Sky News

title: Live for Now
hook: A protest ended with a can of soda.
before: Pepsi wanted a film about unity at a time of real protest in the United States.
idea: In the film, Kendall Jenner leaves a photo shoot, joins a protest and hands a police officer a Pepsi.
shift: Critics said it trivialised protest movements. Pepsi first defended the film, then pulled it and apologised to Jenner.
measure: The time from release to withdrawal. A fact, not a result
evidence: The withdrawal and apology are in Pepsi’s own statement. No public figure shows an effect on sales.
lesson: If a brand borrows a cause, people will ask what it has ever done for it.
test: There is no effectiveness record. The evidence is the reaction and Pepsi’s statement.
links: Read Pepsi’s statement withdrawing the film
memorable: The scene with the can became a meme within hours.

creative.label: Watch the withdrawn Live for Now spot in a Vimeo archive upload
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: The ad every brief about purpose should have to watch first. Nobody in the film had anything at stake.

image.alt: Kendall Jenner handing a can of Pepsi to a police officer in the 2017 advert
image.credit: Pepsi, Live for Now (2017) · film still reproduced by KQED

title: FCK
hook: A chicken chain ran out of chicken and said sorry with three letters.
before: In February 2018 KFC switched delivery companies, chicken didn’t arrive, and hundreds of UK restaurants closed.
idea: Mother London rearranged the logo on an empty bucket to read FCK and ran it as a full-page apology in national newspapers.
shift: The apology became the story. Coverage moved from the closures to the ad.
measure: Articles reported in the agency’s award entry, alongside a social reach of about 1bn
evidence: The figures come from the agency’s award entry and are self-reported reach. No public source shows the effect on sales or reputation.
lesson: An apology works when it sounds like the brand and doesn’t dodge the problem.
test: The record counts coverage and social reach.
links: See the award entry · The One Show
memorable: It is rude, funny and completely honest, which is hard to manage in one word.

creative.label: Watch Mother London’s case film for the FCK print apology at The One Show
creative.heading: Campaign media

metric_label: Articles that carried the ad, self-reported
take: My favourite apology ever written. It said sorry without grovelling, and it never pretended the problem was small.

image.alt: A tipped KFC bucket with its letters rearranged to FCK against a red background
image.credit: KFC and Mother London, FCK (2018) · print artwork reproduced by It’s Nice That

title: The Gift That Gives Back
hook: A Christmas present that people read as an insult.
before: Peloton was growing fast and wanted a Christmas ad about the bike as a gift.
idea: In the ad, a woman records a year of workouts after her husband gives her a Peloton.
shift: Many viewers read it as a husband pushing his wife to lose weight. Peloton said the ad had been misinterpreted. Ryan Reynolds then cast the same actress in an ad for his gin.
measure: The fall in market value on the first trading day after the backlash, as widely reported
evidence: Peloton’s shares fell more than 9% that day. The wider market was also down, so the figure is a trend, not a measure of the ad’s effect.
lesson: People don’t judge an ad by what you meant. They judge it by what they see.
test: The record is the share price and the public reaction.
memorable: Her face. Viewers saw nerves where the brand meant joy.

creative.label: Watch the original 2019 television advert in PRODU’s archive
creative.heading: Campaign media

metric_label: Market value lost in a day
take: The case with the best ending. A rival turned the failure into its own ad within days. That’s what happens when you leave a gap.

image.alt: Monica Ruiz recording herself next to a Peloton bike
image.credit: Peloton, The Gift That Gives Back (2019) · still from the original television spot

title: Women Belong in the Kitchen
hook: A good cause behind a terrible first line.
before: Burger King was launching a scholarship to help women train as chefs, for International Women’s Day.
idea: Its UK account tweeted ‘Women belong in the kitchen’, with the explanation in the replies. The same line ran in a newspaper ad.
shift: Most people saw only the first line. After a day of backlash the tweet was deleted and the brand said, ‘We got our initial tweet wrong and we’re sorry.’
measure: The time between posting and deletion. A fact, not a result
evidence: The deletion and apology are recorded in coverage and in the brand’s own posts. No public figure shows an effect.
lesson: On social, the first line is the whole ad. Nobody reads the thread.
test: There is no effectiveness record. The evidence is the reaction and the apology.
links: See the full-page scholarship advert · B&T
memorable: It is a provocation that only worked for people who read to the end.

creative.label: Watch Global News report on the tweet and Burger King’s apology
creative.heading: Campaign media

take: Clever in a meeting, wrong in a feed. The scholarship was worth talking about, and the joke buried it.

image.alt: Screenshot of the original Burger King UK International Women’s Day tweet
image.credit: Burger King UK, International Women’s Day tweet (2021) · screenshot from Reuters footage published by The Washington Post

title: The Boycott
hook: One social post, and America’s best-selling beer lost the top spot.
before: Bud Light had long been the best-selling beer in the United States.
idea: In April 2023 the brand sent transgender influencer Dylan Mulvaney a personalised can for a sponsored post.
shift: A boycott followed. The company’s response pleased neither critics nor supporters, and by June Modelo Especial had overtaken Bud Light in US retail sales.
measure: The fall in retail sales against the same weeks a year earlier, per Bump Williams data
evidence: Retail data shows a steep fall and the loss of first place. Light beers were already declining, so the boycott isn’t the only cause.
lesson: If you take a stand, stand by it. Backing away loses both sides.
test: Retail sales data tracked weekly sales against the year before.
memorable: It shows how quickly a single post can become a national argument.

creative.label: Watch NBC News report on the response, with excerpts from Dylan Mulvaney’s post
creative.heading: Campaign media

impact_source: Read the sales report · CBS News
metric_label: Retail sales, four weeks to 3 June
take: The partnership wasn’t the failure. The silence afterwards was. A brand that won’t say what it believes leaves everyone else to say it.
data_source: Lost its place as the top beer

image.alt: Dylan Mulvaney with Bud Light and a close-up of the can bearing her portrait
image.credit: Dylan Mulvaney’s sponsored Instagram post (2023) · screenshots reproduced by The Philadelphia Inquirer

title: The Old Timer Goes
hook: A chain took the old man out of its logo, then put him back.
before: Cracker Barrel’s logo showed an old man leaning on a barrel, and its restaurants were full of country nostalgia.
idea: In August 2025 it unveiled a simpler text logo as part of a wider refresh of the brand and its restaurants.
shift: The backlash was huge and political. About a week later the company said it would keep the old logo.
measure: The time from the new logo’s unveiling to the reversal. A fact, not a result
evidence: The reversal is well recorded. Reports of the share price moves vary, and sales were already declining before the change, so no figure isolates the effect.
lesson: When nostalgia is the product, modernising the logo looks like selling the past.
test: The record is the reversal and press coverage.
links: Read about the sales before the change · Fortune
memorable: People defended a cartoon of a man on a barrel as if he were family.

creative.label: Watch WHAS11’s report on the response
creative.heading: News film

impact_source: Read the reversal report · Boston Globe
metric_label: Roughly, before the old logo came back
take: Gap all over again, fifteen years later. Brands keep learning this one the hard way.

image.alt: The short-lived yellow Cracker Barrel logo with only the wordmark
image.credit: Cracker Barrel, August 2025 logo · Heidi Pearce / brand press kit on MultiVu
